newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major battered by Europe, sleaze.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major battered by Europe, sleaze.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives were rocked on Wednesday by the resignation of a minister in a parliamentary sleaze row and fresh divisions over Europe.

The bitterly divided ruling party faced the prospect of becoming a minority government this week, with the opposition Labour Party expected to win a by-election in northern England and wipe out Major's one-seat majority.
With a general election due some time before next May, the Conservative Party is trailing Labour by 37 points, according to the latest opinion poll.

David Willetts resigned his ministerial post as Paymaster General -- responsible for planning and presentation of government policy -- after being criticised by fellow members of parliament investigating allegations of so-called "sleaze".

Willetts, a top government strategist, quit after the release of a report which said he had not been "frank and open" in evidence to a parliamentary committee investigating whether MPs took cash to ask parliamentary questions for businessmen.
The report by the Standards and Privileges Committee came close to accusing Willetts of lying, which would have meant his suspension or expulsion as a member of parliament.
In any event, he was the ninth minister to quit as a result of a scandal since Major won the last election in 1992.

In parliament, finance minister Kenneth Clarke ran into more trouble from anti-European Conservatives when he sought to defend the government's "wait and see" policy on whether or not to join a single European currency.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke said Britain was right to keep its options open on whether or not to join economic and monetary union (EMU), due to begin in 1999.
But he was jeered by "Eurosceptic" Conservatives when he told them getting rid of the pound sterling would not mean joining a European superstate.
That argument, as Clarke opened a two-day debate on the European Union, failed to convince leading Conservative Eurosceptic Tony Marlow.
"Why do you think the vast majority of the Conservative Party is against the single currency. It is precisely because it would be the end of the nation state," Marlow said.

As his majority has dwindled, Major has been forced to pay more attention to the voice of the "Eurosceptics", who want him at least to rule out British entry into the single currency for the next five years.

Major technically lost his one-seat majority last week when a disaffected member of parliament withdrew his support over the closure of a hospital emergency ward. But the MP did not officially abandon the party.
But when the votes are counted in the safe Labour seat of Barnsley East in the early hours of Friday, the Conservatives will officially be a minority government.
Labour is not expected to move at once to a vote of no confidence as the Conservataves could rely on the support of nine pro-British Northern Ireland Ulster Unionists.
But Labour can make life tough for the Conservatives in parliamentary committees which scrutinise legislation.
